title: Adoro te devote
hookLine: Hopkins translated it: Godhead here in hiding, whom I do adore

lines: A POET AND A LATIN HYMN.
cards: A poet sits with a Latin hymn and tries to carry it over into English without spilling any. The poet is Gerard Manley Hopkins, a Jesuit priest whose own poems bend English into strange new music.
The hymn is one tradition credits to Thomas Aquinas, a quiet prayer before the Eucharist. Its first words are Adoro te devote: I adore you devoutly.
And Hopkins opens with a line that turns a doctrine into a picture: Godhead here in hiding, whom I do adore. Yesterday's hymns were for processions and choirs. This one is for one person, kneeling.

teach.b: The Latin opening: "Adoro te devote, latens Deitas." I adore you devoutly, hidden Godhead. Latens means lying hidden.
The whole hymn is built on that: God present, but out of sight. Scripture knew the idea. Isaiah, in the Douay-Rheims: "Verily thou art a hidden God, the God of Israel the saviour."
Then the second verse goes straight at the senses: "Visus, tactus, gustus in te fallitur."

Sight, touch and taste are deceived in you. Here's a wrinkle. Two days ago, in the Summa, Thomas was careful to say the senses are not deceived at Mass, because the appearances of bread really are there.

The hymn speaks from the pew: the eyes see bread, the tongue tastes bread, and they can't reach what's underneath. Some readers put it this way: one is explaining; the other is kneeling. So what's left to trust?
The hymn answers: hearing. "Sed auditu solo tuto creditur."
Only by hearing is it safely believed.
Hearing the word of Christ, who said this is my body. Paul, in Romans: "Faith then cometh by hearing; and hearing by the word of Christ."

teach.h: VERILY THOU ART A HIDDEN GOD.
teach.b: The hymn goes on, in effect: I believe whatever the Son of God has said, for nothing is truer than Truth's own word.
That's the whole movement of the prayer: the eyes come up empty, the ears catch a word, and the heart bows. Scholars have debated whether Thomas wrote it himself; tradition keeps his name on it.
Either way, it sounds like someone who spent his life thinking about what can't be seen.

how: Catholics pray the Adoro te devote during Eucharistic adoration and before or after Communion, either in Latin or in English versions, including Hopkins's translation.

games.q: you're praying before the host. your eyes see bread and your tongue tastes bread. what does the hymn say to trust?

practice: If you pray, say the first verse slowly, in Latin if you know it or in Hopkins's English, or just the opening, Adoro te devote, latens Deitas, and let it sit.
If you don't pray, take the line Godhead here in hiding and notice one thing near you that's real but can't be seen: love in a house, trust in a friendship, air in the room.
